Question: What happened to the cats that Schrodinger used in his experiments about quantum physics? Would such experiments be allowed today under animal testing laws?
Answer: The cat in question was gifted to the Tollan (an alien humanoid species) named Narim, who at first expressed shock that such a cruel experiment was allowed in the first place. But then he was assured that no, the experiment itself was just a thought experiment, not something carried out in real life. The cat was actually named Schrödinger, not experimented on by Schrödinger. Narim also expressed bemusement once he understood that Earth science is still so far behind, we actually take the probabilistic Copenhagen interpretation (which he calls “Kulivrian physics”, one of the “misconceptions of elementary science”) seriously. All this of course took place in the fictitious universe of the television series Stargate SG-1. In the real world, the famous cat was used as a (fictitious) example by Schrödinger, demonstrating that taking the probabilistic interpretation a tad too far might yield strange conclusions. Question: If gravity is a bend in spacetime, why do objects fall straight rather than in a curved or parabolic direction?
Answer: Did you say spacetime? Very well, let’s look at a falling rock in spacetime. Let me draw a diagram using the horizontal axis as time, the vertical axis as space (altitude above ground), illustrating a falling object in a gravitational field, accelerating vertically toward the ground. This is the trajectory of a vertically falling rock in space and time as it is dropped from 125 meters in the standard gravitational field of the Earth. After five seconds, the rock would be about to hit the ground. Certainly does not look straight to me. In the absence of gravity, however, the trajectory would be illustrated by a straight horizontal line, as the rock’s position would remain unchanged as time passes. Question: If we accept that dark matter exist, they must be part of the entire planet Earth, including living plant and animal organisms. In this case, is it correct to believe that dark matter is part of the human organism?
Answer: If dark matter exists, it is indeed presumed to be present everywhere, though its density is very low compared to terrestrial densities. However, I’d hesitate to call it a “part of”, e.g., organisms. By way of an example that is known to exist with certainty, right now there are countless neutrinos going through your body. Are they part of your body? Not really. Why? Because neutrinos are effectively non-interacting. To them, your body might as well not be there. And vice versa, for your body the presence of the neutrinos makes no difference. Neutrinos still interact with ordinary matter though, just very, very, very weakly. An awful lot of neutrinos would be needed to make a noticeable difference. Sure, if you happened to be situated near an exploding supernova, the neutrino flux might be enough to evaporate you in an instant, but for that, the explosion of an entire giant star would be required, fairly close to you. In contrast, the millions, billions, trillions of neutrinos that pass through your body right this moment make no difference whatsoever. They are not part of you. The presumed dark matter of cosmology interacts even less with ordinary matter. So even if it is present right here, right now, it is not part of you, of animals, plants, or the Earth. It happens to be in the same place in space at the same time, but it might as well be in another galaxy far, far away: There is no interaction, no connection between that dark matter medium and your body. So no, whether or not dark matter exists remains to be seen, but it is definitely not part of the human body. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: Why is it so hard to believe WW2 happened for those who didn't live through it, why is WW2 so movie like in many ways?
Answer: I did not live through WW2, but it is certainly not hard to believe or movie-like for me. I was born in Budapest, nearly 20 years after the war ended. Yet I grew up in a city where, especially in the smaller side streets, the scars of war were still all too readily visible. Damaged facades, bullet holes were everywhere in those old, turn-of-the-century mostly brick-and-mortar apartment buildings. (Many still have the scars in poorer, less well-maintained parts of the city or in spots not readily visible from the outside, such as internal courtyards.) And some historical buildings were still very much in ruins, such as those on historic Castle Hill on the Buda side. Another thing that was not terribly uncommon as I was growing up was the discovery of unexploded ordnance. Radio newscasts telling us that a street, an intersection was temporarily evacuated while bomb disposal teams were on scene neutralizing the threat. Still happens, by the way, though it’s much more of a rarity nowadays. More than that, my Mom lived through the siege of the city as small girl. She has many memories that she shared with me: The air raids that sent the family to the bomb shelter at Christmas, the damaged, looted apartment to which they returned many weeks later, corpses of humans and also horses, the latter sometimes surrounded by people who were carving them up for the meat. My grandmother still lived in that same apartment when I was growing up. She had a container, a large, shiny, repurposed aluminum can that she used to store flour. The can bore English-language markings courtesy of the American Red Cross, part of a post-war aid package to help a starving population. While my Mom and her family were hiding in that shelter, my father, much older, struggled to help his Jewish first wife and child and Jewish business partner with forged documents, which kept them out of the ghetto and ultimately, quite possibly kept them off the trains heading for Auschwitz. He could have been caught, carrying forged, still blank passports for instance when he was once stopped by an Arrow Cross patrol in late 1944. He was lucky: they did not search him. And of course the country I grew up in was at the time still occupied by forces of the USSR, the country that liberated the eastern half of Europe from Nazism, only to install their own version of totalitarianism in its place. So no, although (thankfully) I did not live through WW2, it is definitely not movie-like for me. People I knew, people close to me, but also places, buildings, streets all carried, sometimes still carry, tangible memories of that war.

Question: Why are black holes called black holes if they are actually white or lighter than the space around them?
Answer: They are neither white nor lighter than the space around them. In classical general relativity, a black hole is truly black: it absorbs all light that hits it, and emits absolutely nothing. You really cannot get more black than that. Even with Hawking radiation, the situation is similar. Sure, black holes radiate. But astrophysical black holes have Hawking temperatures that are just a tiny, tiny fraction of the temperature of the cosmic microwave background radiation. In other words, even in this case, the black hole is a lot more black than the cosmos: it absorbs many orders of magnitude more radiation than it emits. So that’s why they are called black. Again, you really cannot get more black than these things. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: What would it look like if gravitational waves came at us and were strong enough to be visible? Like if two ton618 sized black holes collided nearby. Just so that the wave could make a visible distortion in space. What would it look like?
Answer: Visible is the wrong word to use here as there’s nothing to see. However, you might hear it! Let us assume a “clean” collision, two black holes with no other material, so no visible light, no gamma rays, nothing that would kill you or vaporize you, just gravitational waves. And you get close enough. Well, when the merger is between two stellar black holes, the peak gravitational wave emission happens at frequencies that fall well within the audible range. Which means that if you are close enough (but not too close!), you might actually hear (literally, hear) the result, as the passing time-varying tidal effect moves wiggles parts of your body, including all those little bits inside your ear. The technical nature of the waves (transversal waves traveling at the vacuum speed of light) is different from sound waves (longitudinal pressure waves in a medium, traveling much slower than the vacuum speed of light) but the effect is similar: mechanical excitation of bits that are particularly sensitive to the frequencies in question. Mind you, don’t get too close: Just as a powerful blast of sound waves can kill you, so can a too powerful gravitational wave. Now that’s two stellar black holes. You mentioned TON 618. They are much too big for anything audible to happen. The frequencies in question would be measured in a microhertz or less, which is to say, a period measured in days. You would neither hear nor see anything until you are close enough to experience powerful tides on a time scale of days. So if such an event were to occur in our relative stellar neighborhood, the effect could be an unexplained tide, which, depending on how close we are to the event, could be minor or devastating. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How is the speed of gravity determined?
Answer: First of all, while I recognize that this is a bit of semantics, there is no “speed of gravity” any more than there is a “speed of electromagnetism”. Gravity is an interaction, it does not have an inherent speed. However, influences in the gravitational field, far from sources, travel as transverse waves, and these indeed do have a speed. Theory tells us that this speed is the same as the speed of influences in the electromagnetic field, i.e., electromagnetic waves such as light. While few had real doubts that this prediction is valid, its first observational test came seven years ago with the LIGO event GW170817. This gravitational wave event turned out to be the collision and merger of a pair of neutron stars, an event that was also detectable in a multitude of electromagnetic frequencies. The electromagnetic and gravitational signals arrived at the same time, even though they event took place some 130 million light years from here. This tells us that indeed, gravitational and electromagnetic waves traveled at the same speed. As a matter of fact, this had a direct impact on theory. There are proposed alternative theories of gravitation in which there is not one but two (or more) metrical fields, one determining the speed of gravitational waves, the other, the speed of electromagnetic waves. These “bimetric” theories were essentially falsified by the GW170817 observation.

Question: Why do people who use the metric system assume that 9meters is 32 feet when gravity is really 9.81m per sec per sec?
Answer: Well, for starters, “gravity” is not really 9.81 m/s^2. What is 9.81 m/s^2 is the average gravitational acceleration at sea level on a minor planet called Earth in one of the popular languages spoken by its inhabitants. The units in this expression were historically derived from the actual properties of the same planet (notably, its size and its rate of rotation) but that’s beside the point. In a small number of places on this planet, however, inhabitants prefer to use a different unit for length, originally inspired by the typical size of one of their appendages they call “feet”. The conversion factor is a simple one: 1 foot equals 0.3048 meters or conversely, 1 m = (1/0.3048) ft. The rest is easily done by way of using a calculator: 9.81 m / s^2 = 9.81 (1/0.3048) ft / s^2 = 9.81/0.3048 ft / s^2 = 32.2 ft / s^2, rounded to three significant digits in the decimal number system these inhabitants prefer (undoubtedly because their forepaws happen to have ten appendages in total, called “digits”). This simple calculation should not challenge any of the adult or near-adult inhabitants of the aforementioned planet, whether or not they are regular users of what they call the metric system or other systems of measurement. Utilizing the same skills and a calculating device, they can also easily calculate that 9 m = (9 / 0.3048) ft = 29.527559 ft to a reasonable number of decimal digits. Indeed, most of the inhabitants master the necessary skill set in an institution called “grade school”. Yes, I know, strange planet. Question: A system composed by a piece of iron and a magnet has more energy if the iron is closer the magnet. So, the overall weight should be (very very slightly) different. Is there an intuitive thought experiment to show it?
Answer: Actually, when you bring a piece of iron to a magnet, the system has less energy when the iron is closer to the magnet. You need to invest energy, do work to separate the iron from the magnet. The amount of energy is usually minuscule so it is not something we can measure, but to offer an intuition: Suppose you have a magnet and you release a piece of iron nearby. The magnet attracts it: the piece of iron accelerates, gaining kinetic energy at the expense of losing potential energy. The overall energy-content of the system remains the same. Then finally, the piece of iron hits the magnet and stops moving. Its kinetic energy now transforms into the random motion of its and the magnet’s molecules, i.e., it gets converted into heat. That heat is then radiated away into the environment as both the piece of iron and the magnet cool down th ambient temperature. The amount of energy lost by way of that waste heat radiated away is precisely the amount by which the mass-energy of the system decreases. Of course as I said, the amount is minuscule. Far, far less than what we could possibly measure even with our most sensitive instruments. However, similar processes that go on either on the nuclear scale (much large energies) or simply on a much larger mass scale (e.g., astrophysical systems) do have measurable properties that explicitly confirm this description. Going back to the piece of iron and the magnet, to remove the piece of iron the process needs to be reversed. A force must be applied to separate the piece of iron from the magnet and move it some distance away. The work done by this force is now the potential energy of the system, i.e., its ability to make the piece of iron move again if it were to be released, allowed again to accelerate towards the magnet. Question: What is quantum? Which things fit the definition of quantum?
Answer: There are things that are “quantized”, which is to say, exhibit behavior that comes in distinct chunks, and the branch of physics that deals with these things is called therefore “quantum physics”. But to the extent that it even touches on the concept of “quantum”, it’s a consequence, not a foundation. Not anymore. At first, quantum physics was mostly empirical. Yes, it was based on the idea that atoms emit or absorb energy in such discrete chunks, or quanta. This was observed. This led, for instance, to Planck’s famous radiation law, which marks the dawn of quantum physics. But over time, we became a tad more sophisticated. Less then thirty years after Planck initiated his revolution, the “new” quantum theory of Heisenberg and Schrödinger emerged. It was no longer about atoms emitting and absorbing quanta, but something far more fundamental: the mathematical representation of the state of a physical system. In classical physics, constituent parts of a physical system can be characterized by a) where they are, b) how they move. In other words, their positions and their speed (or momenta). These can be represented by numbers. A position is just a set of coordinates. A velocity is a vector that can be characterized by a set of coordinates. As I said, numbers. Then comes the “new” quantum mechanics, which represents positions and momenta by… well, something else. Matrices in Heisenberg’s case, function operators in Schrödinger’s, but the bottom line is the same: These things are not numbers. Specifically, they do not behave like numbers do under multiplication. Take the momenta p and positions q of a system. In classical physics, we can multiply these numbers together and get a result that does not depend on the order of multiplication: p q = q p , or p q − q p = 0. But this is not how positions and momenta behave in the new quantum physics. They obey instead the relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , where ℏ is the reduced Planck constant and, well, i = √ − 1 . This leads to all sorts of weird consequences, which have been confirmed experimentally. Among other things… well, quanta. Take one of the simplest physical systems, a simple oscillator (the so-called harmonic oscillator). Describe it in terms of these non-commuting variables and you get a weird result: The oscillator cannot have arbitrary energies. Its energy is discretized, going up or down by one unit, or quantum at a time. Electrons in an atom are well described by such oscillators as a mathematical model. So there we have it, the quantized behavior of how atoms emit or absorb energy. But quantum physics in general is not really about quanta. It’s not about chopping things up into small units. That might have been the original inspiration more than a century ago, but it has become something much more nuanced. Planck’s quanta are still there, but as a consequence, not as a building block, of the theory. There are plenty of “quantum” systems that have no quantized behavior. E.g., a free particle can have any energy; nothing “quantized” there. The fundamental statement of the theory is not about quanta; it is about the behavior of those key variables, the positions and momenta of a physical system, and how this behavior is described by the mathematics of noncommuting things, as opposed to the mathematics of simple numbers. Like it or not, that is how Nature behaves, as demonstrated by countless experiments. That said, when we go beyond simple quantum mechanics into the realm of quantum field theory, things change a bit. A field, like the electromagnetic field, can be described as a sum of, well, pure waves really, by way of what is called a Fourier-transform. Each of these pure waves behaves like a harmonic oscillator, which we know how to describe using quantum physics. Each of these harmonic oscillators is characterized by those distinct chunks of energy by which the oscillator’s energy can increase or decrease. In quantum field theory, these distinct chunks of energy (and possibly other conserved properties, like charge or angular momentum) turn out to be none other than the things we’ve know, we’ve observed, as particles! So there you have it: elementary particles come closest to the concept of “quantum”. (Indeed, sometimes we even say so explicitly: e.g., “photons are the quanta of the electromagnetic field.”) If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: If excitations in the "electron field” look to us like electrons and positrons, and excitations in the "photon field” look to us like photons, what do we perceive excitations in the "electric field" or "magnetic field" or "gravitational field" as?
Answer: Electric and magnetic fields are both manifestations of the electromagnetic field (i.e., the “photon field”). How the electromagnetic field appears to split into these components is observer-dependent. For instance, an observer standing next to an electron will see an electrostatic field and no magnetic field; another, moving observer, looking at the same charge, would see a time-varying electric field in his moving reference frame, along with a magnetic field. Whether or not the gravitational field is a quantum field remains an open question. If it is a quantum field, we expect that its excitations would, under the right circumstances, appear as “gravitons”. However, given how weak the gravitational interaction is, we may never be able to “perceive” gravitons directly with any conceivable present or future experiment. There are occasionally proposals though that might (or not) help us confirm the quantum nature of the gravitational field. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: If an airliner (e.g. Boeing 747 800) was magically transported to the same altitude as the International Space Station, how quickly would it depressurise?
Answer: It would be surprisingly slow. Keep in mind that at normal cruising attitude, outside pressure is already pretty low, less than 20% of sea level pressure. So the pressure-induced stress on the aircraft fuselage at ~400 km altitude (where the ISS orbits) would not be much greater than during cruise. So nothing dramatic happens… other than, of course, all engines failing due to lack of air, along with any auxiliary power units (APUs), so the only things operating on that aircraft at this time would be minimum emergency equipment running off battery power. Having said that, assuming that the aircraft is properly pressurized and there are no undue leaks or valves left open, the leakage rate of a well-maintained aircraft seems to be surprisingly low. I found some data: According to a conversation at PPRuNe Forums, it took some 30 minutes to reach a cabin pressure altitude of 10,000 ft in one new aircraft. In the same conversation, someone else quotes 500 ft/min as the leakage rate of a brand new A320. So even a conservative guesstimate suggests at least 15 minutes before pressure drops within that fuselage to dangerously low levels. Which creates an interesting scenario. If that aircraft was magically lifted to 400 km altitude without being accelerated to orbital speed, it won’t stay up that high for very long. Rather, it’d start to fall, and fall rather rapidly since there is no noticeable air resistance. In fact, without air resistance it would reach the ground in something like 5 minutes. Of course in reality, it would run into denser and denser air that would ultimately slow its descent. The question is, would it be survivable? No, it’s not about heat shields. Heat shields are needed for spacecraft re-entry because they enter the atmosphere at orbital speed. This hypothetical aircraft of ours would start off slow, and never reach speeds at which heating due air resistance becomes a major concern. Even so, it probably (almost certainly?) would not survive, especially considering that at this point, the pilots have no control over the aircraft; there is no power, and of course no air for the control surfaces to operate on. Before the pilots can do anything useful, the airplane would have to descend to an altitude where there is enough oxygen to start up at least an APU. That would be, what, maybe 20 km or less? Far too late. Much earlier, the aircraft would be falling at supersonic speeds, at an uncontrolled attitude, encountering denser and denser layers of air. (Recall that the space shuttle Columbia broke up at an altitude of ~60 km; it was much faster of course, but it should tell you that even at 60 km, there’s already more than enough air to cause structural failure for a fast-falling aircraft.) However, if by some miracle, that aircraft makes it to 20–25 km altitude without losing important bits like a wing or two, and an APU could be restarted, I think it is conceivable that the pilots might be able to regain control and slow the aircraft down without substantially more structural damage, as it continues to descend. I have no idea (I don’t think anyone does) how a 747 would fly at Mach 3 at 20–25 km but who knows, perhaps it would manage to stay attached to most of its wings as the pilots bleed altitude and speed? (I am thinking of China Airlines Flight 006 as I am writing down these somewhat optimistic words.) The point is, should that miracle happen, during the 5–10 minute ordeal at no time would cabin pressure drop to a level that would seriously harm or kill the occupants, unless something else (structural failure, a stuck valve, etc.) causes the cabin to depressurize rapidly at an altitude that is still too high for the oxygen masks to be effective (above ~20 km outside pressure is low enough for our blood to boil at body temperature). The big if is whether or not the airplane would survive the fall through the upper atmosphere in one piece; and the answer is that it almost certainly would not. Question: Viktor T. Toth said that life on Earth is made possible by the low enthropy energy we receive from the Sun. What is meant by “low enthropy energy” and in what sense is it necessary for creating and maintaining life on Earth?
Answer: As per the second law of thermodynamics, entropy cannot decrease in a closed system. Entropy is a measure of disorder: A disordered system will not spontaneously become ordered. The more disordered a system is, the higher its entropy. Life, ultimately, is about disordered raw materials combining to form complex, highly ordered structures. This represents a significant decrease in entropy. That decrease in entropy must be balanced, in turn, by an increase in entropy somewhere else, and the two systems must be connected. That somewhere else is the Sun. The Earth receives, from the Sun, energy mostly in the form of visible light, photons at (roughly) 6000 K (degrees kelvin). In turn, the Earth radiates into deep space energy mostly in the form of thermal infrared, photons at (roughly) 300 K. That means that for each incoming photon from the Sun, the Earth radiates about 20 photons into deep space. (The two must be in balance otherwise the Earth would boil or freeze, due to excess thermal energy or a deficit in thermal energy.) It goes without saying that 20 photons can represent a lot more disorder, a lot more randomness than 1 photon. In other words, the energy that the Earth receives from the Sun has a lot less entropy than the thermal “waste heat” that the Earth radiates into deep space. Some of the incoming solar energy is captured by living things, either directly (plants) or indirectly (e.g., humans eating a potato). This represents a low entropy source, allowing those living systems to become organized, create complexity, and radiate away excess energy in the form of higher entropy waste heat. But it need not be even about living things. Just imagine a simple machine that uses the heat from the Sun to boil water, which then drives a piston, which does useful work through a mechanism (e.g., a crane, lifting bricks to build a house, turning disorder into order). The used up steam, released from the piston, is allowed to recondense, its waste heat radiated into the sky (deep space), the water ready to be reused in the next cycle. If there was no “high entropy sink” (the sky), we could not recondense the water and the machine would eventually stop when its water reservoir is emptied. The biological cycle may be a tad more sophisticated than a simple solar steam engine driving a crane, but the thermodynamic principles are exactly the same. Question: What is the propagator for a massless scalar field, and how can you compute it using C++?
Answer: The propagator for a massless scalar field, which obeys the Klein-Gordon equation ∂ μ ∂ μ ϕ = 0 , can be derived from the Green’s function of this equation, ∂ μ ∂ μ G ( x − y ) = δ 4 ( x − y ) that, in momentum space, becomes − k 2 ~ G ( k ) = − 1 , hence ~ G ( k ) = 1 k 2 + i ϵ , where we introduced a small imaginary term, as usual, to avoid the singularity at k = 0. By itself, this expression is not something you would compute numerically in a language such as C++. You may be able to derive expressions of this sort in computer algebra (either general purpose CAS with specialized packages or special purpose systems). The propagator is used in combination with the vertex rules of a theory to compute cross-sections corresponding to particle interactions. That computation itself may not be trivial as it involves divergent integrals that may need to be regularized in order to obtain meaningful results for observable quantities. In short, no, unless you first use C++ to build a CAS for quantum field theory, you would not be using C++ for this type of computation. You might use a CAS to derive an expression for an observable quantity that you then import into a C++ program for numerical evaluation (perhaps as part of a larger computation) but the propagator on its own is not something you’d likely use in C++. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Would you rather touch antimatter or a black hole?
Answer: You’d have to explain to me first how one could accomplish either, even if the consequences are ignored. A black hole’s event horizon is forever in the future. That means that to touch it, you either a) live forever, or b) actually fall into the black hole. Except that falling into the black hole, with the exception of some of the very largest supermassive black holes, means certain death even before you reach the horizon, because tidal forces will rip your body apart. In short, you cannot touch a black hole. And how do you touch antimatter? OK, technically if you’re eating a banana right now, chances are you’re “touching” some antimatter, the occasional positron that comes as a rare decay product of the K-40 isotope that can be found in living things, including bananas. But presumably, you meant “bulk” antimatter, such as a visible quantity of some antimatter liquid or solid. So the first question that pops into mind is… how is it stored? How is it isolated from the environment so that it doesn’t already go kaboom? OK, so maybe it’s a piece of antimatter iron, floating in deep space. Except that even in deep interplanetary space, there is matter: the occasional molecule of gas, even microscopic dust particles here and there. Still if you insist… I suppose you could float over to where that anti-iron piece is, and grab it with your hands, while wearing a spacesuit with gloves. Oops, that would be your kaboom moment. I suppose this is nonetheless a less unpleasant way to go though than being ripped apart by relativistic tides. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can antimatter be considered as "visible matter" because it can interact with light even though it has the opposite charge of normal matter?
Answer: Absolutely. In the context of cosmological physics, matter and antimatter are both “ordinary”, visible matter, made up of particles that interact with each other and with the electromagnetic field. Dark matter does not interact with the electromagnetic field (or if it does, it does so very, very, very weakly) and does not interact with normal matter (which includes antimatter). We don’t know what dark matter is (we cannot even be sure that it exists) but if there is such a thing, this is its defining characteristic. In contrast, antimatter very much interacts with normal matter. So much so, that this is how we know that even distant regions of the visible universe are dominated by normal matter, not antimatter. How do we know? Matter is everywhere, there are hydrogen atoms even in intergalactic space. If there were, e.g., distant galaxy clusters made of antimatter, the boundary region between antimatter and normal matter regions would “glow” in the gamma ray part of the spectrum from the occasional matter-antimatter interactions. Granted, in the very low density intergalactic medium, such collisions would be infrequent, but on the other hand, the volumes are ginormous, and the resulting gamma ray background would be observable.

Question: What is the Higgs field explained simply?
Answer: The Higgs field is one of the fields of the Standard Model of particle physics. What do particles have to do with fields? Well, in a quantum field theory, “particles” are quantized excitations (units of energy) in a field. Take the electromagnetic field, for instance. Light is electromagnetic radiation. It is a wave: countless experiments demonstrate its wave-like properties. Yet when we let light interact with a sensor, we find that the energy-content of the electromagnetic field is transferred to the sensor one unit of energy, one “photon” at a time. (Confusingly, this is *not* what people are talking about when they discuss wave-particle duality.) So in this sense, the Higgs field is just like the electromagnetic field; the field of electrons; the fields associated with other charge leptons, quarks, neutrinos, vector bosons, gluons. Fields interact. E.g., the field of electrons can interact with the electromagnetic field: we experience this, e.g., when an excitation of the electron field, i.e., a charged electron, accelerates and this creates electromagnetic radiation. The Higgs field interacts with other fields, too.. But the Higgs field has one additional curious property. Usually, a field is at its lowest energy state when it has no excitations. The Higgs is different: Its lowest energy state is an excited state. It has a nonzero “vacuum expectation value”. What this implies, however, is that the vacuum (containing the Higgs field with no excitations) can decay into a new vacuum state, in which the Higgs field has some excitations, but the overall energy-content is lower. This has very serious implications, because in this new configuration, we now have other particles interacting with what appears to be the vacuum, which contains these Higgs excitations! The effect of this is that these other particles, which originally had no rest masses, now have potential energy by way of these interactions. And as we know, energy is mass. This is how several particles of the Standard Model become massive. And the reason why this is important is that by starting with originally massless particles, the Standard Model can be mathematically consistent (it can be “renormalized”) yet in the end, thanks to the Higgs field, it yields massive particles after all. As an important side note, I should mention that the Higgs has nothing to do with gravity (not directly; gravity is sourced by energy-content, but the Higgs coupling is not in any way special in this regard) and roughly 99% of the mass of ordinary matter has nothing to do with the Higgs mechanism (it is the energy-content due to the strong interaction binding energy.) Question: If gravitons actually exist - is the gravitational constant the quantum of the force carrier action, which relates the energy carried by a bundle of gravitational force to its frequency?
Answer: No, a coupling constant is not a quantum of anything. A coupling constant determines how strongly two independent fields (in this case, the gravitational field and matter fields) couple to each other, i.e., how strongly they influence one another. The fact that the gravitational constant is not a mere number but it has units attached to it makes it particularly interesting. It means that we can always choose a set of measurement units in which G=1 and it simply disappears from the equations. At the same time, this plays a major rule in the difficulties associated with creating a viable theory of quantum gravity: “naive” quantization leads to a theory that misbehaves at high energies, with infinities that cannot be removed or tamed by reasonable mathematics. Other than that, though, it’s just a coupling constant. It measures how strongly (or weakly, as in this case) matter fields and the gravitational field couple to one another. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is there a semantic difference between the redshift caused by gravity wells and the redshift caused by the expansion of space?
Answer: First of all, allow me to take exception at the (granted, commonly used) expression, “expansion of space”. Space is not a thing. More specifically, it does not have any little markers attached to it by which its expansion, if any, could even be measured! No, it is things (galaxies, gas, dust, etc.) that are flying apart. It is the density of matter that decreases over time. And it is the gravitational field that changes as a result: a physical field that, however, can also be interpreted as the metric of spacetime. It is when folks take this interpretation a little too literally and a little too dogmatically that we end up with “expansion of space”. So then, putting these qualms aside… redshift happens as a result of the relationship between the world lines of the transmitter and the receiver. If the distance (the actual distance, which may be measurable by means of exchanging light signals, for instance) between the transmitter and the receiver changes over time, there is a velocity-induced Doppler frequency shift. If clocks at the different locations (or times!) tick at different rates, there is a gravity-induced redshift (gravity manifests itself primarily in the form of time dilation in general relativity, i.e., the rates at which clocks tick relative to one another.) It is time dilation that yields an observed redshift for light coming from a gravitational well, and it is predominantly time dilation when it comes to the redshift of “high-z” objects, that is, objects very far from here with substantial redshifts. There are some qualitative differences: when it comes to a gravitational well, we’re basically looking at a static configuration, and simply the fact that clocks deep inside that gravitational well tick slower, right now, than clocks elsewhere. When it comes to cosmological redshift, what we see is that in the distant past, matter was much denser, consequently the average gravitational potential was greater and clocks were ticking more slowly back then than they tick today. So truly, it’s gravitational redshift in both cases, just two distinct scenarios: One is the gravitational redshift due to a compact object’s gravitational field here and now, the other is gravitational redshift due to the average gravitational field characterizing the cosmos in the distant past. But fundamentally, it’s gravity in both cases. A consequence of Einstein’s field equations that connect, no, not the “geometry of spacetime” but rather, the tensor field of gravitation with the stress-energy-momentum of matter. It’s due to the weak equivalence principle that we can interpret the tensor field of gravitation as geometry, but as I stressed in many of my answers in the past, Einstein himself cautioned against taking this interpretation too literally. Otherwise it becomes an obstacle, preventing us from thinking about alternate theories of gravity that may not obey the weak equivalence principle, or quantizing gravity as a force. Einstein himself never stopped referring to gravity as a force, the utility of the geometric interpretation notwithstanding. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can Schrodinger's equation be proven to accurately describe quantum mechanics? Are there alternative methods for dealing with quantum mechanics?
Answer: Schrödinger’s equation defines nonrelativistic quantum mechanics. It can be deduced from the classical Hamiltonian, or from the canonical commutation relation p q − q p = − i ℏ , but either way: nonrelativistic quantum mechanics is Schrödinger’s equation. It’s not “proven” (never will be) beyond showing that the math is self-consistent; is is validated when experiments confirm the equation’s predictions. There are, of course, alternatives. There is relativistic quantum particle mechanics in the form of Dirac’s equation. There is relativistic quantum field theory, which kind of implies either the Dirac or the Schrödinger equation in the appropriate limit. And then there are tentative theoretical approaches that attempt to generalize the commutation relation, e.g., by introducing a length scale. The Dirac equation and quantum field theory (in the form of the Standard Model of particle physics) are mathematically self-consistent and are validated by experiment. Alternatives, not so much. Even when the math itself is robust, there is no validation in the form of observational evidence. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Question: If a light ray of white light is bent by the gravity of a massive object like a star, does the light ray undergo diffraction and turn into a rainbow?
Answer: No, it does not, and that is a very important point. The refractive index of transparent materials tends to depend on wavelength. That is to say, light rays of different color will travel at different speeds in that material, and therefore follow different paths. This is why a lens, a prism can split a white ray of light into its constituent colors, creating a rainbow pattern. Gravitational lensing is different, and this has to do fundamentally with the weak equivalence principle. Gravitation is an “equal opportunity” interaction: It does not care about the material properties of the thing that is affected by it. Two rays of light following identical trajectories will be deflected by an identical amount, regardless of their color. This would not be the case, mind you, if the speed of light itself depended on wavelength. And that would be the case if light was a result of an interaction mediated by a particle with mass. But electromagnetism, the interaction behind light, is not mediated by a massive particle. It is mediated by photons, which are massless, so always travel at the vacuum speed of light regardless of their kinetic energy (which in turn determines their frequency, i.e., their color.) So red light and blue light, for instance, despite being substantially different in terms of the energy of the individual photons, will follow the same path in a gravitational field. Having said all that, it is still possible for a gravitational field to produce a rainbow-like effect, but for a different reason. Here is an example of a simulated projection by a gravitational lens with that is not perfectly spherical (i.e., it has a quadrupole mass moment), of light from a point source onto a projection surface: The reason why the colors of the rainbow appear in this image is not because the gravitational lens affected light of different color differently. Rather, it has to do with the constructive/destructive interference of the light wavefront as it arrives at the projection surface; the peaks and valleys of this interference pattern are wavelength-dependent, so we see, e.g., red peaks vs. blue peaks at different locations. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How do you manually compute sin, cos, or tan of any number? Something like sin 10, tan 13, cos 45.092?
Answer: First of all, I would restrict myself to positive angles less than 45 degrees. For other angles, I’d use trigonometric identities. Next, I’d convert angles to radians. This is important. To a reasonable approximation, it amounts to dividing angles (expressed in degrees) by 57.3. This means that the largest angle in radians that I’ll be dealing with will be π / 4 or about 0.785, so well below 1. Now I can use the Taylor series for the sine: sin x ≃ x − x 3 / 6... OK, let’s give it a try. Suppose you are asking me to compute the sine of 70 degrees. But 70 is greater than 45, so I’ll be computing the sine of 20 degrees instead, which is the cosine of 70 degrees. Converting to radians by dividing with 57.3, I get 0.349. To three decimals, 0.349 − 0.349 3 / 6 will be 0.342. Since this is the cosine of 70 degrees, I can calculate the sine by taking the square root of 1 − 0.342 2 = 0.883. There are ways of calculating the square root similar to long division, so it can be done on paper… or just use trial and error. The result is 0.940. So let’s double-check with a calculator: I get 0.93969262. Bingo! Mind you, this is not a very efficient thing to do, especially if you need a lot of trigonometry. You might be better off using a slide rule or a table of trig functions. Which were the common methods used by engineers before the advent of electronic calculators back in the 1970s*. Indeed, if you were to find yourself in a post-apocalyptic wasteland with all electronics dead and rotting away, and you are tasked with rebuilding civilization one calculation at a time, you might do yourself a favor pre-calculating sines and cosines (and exponentials and logarithms and square roots and the like) and create a set of nice tables for later use. *Or later. I sometimes calculated trig functions using this approach on the four-function calculator that was a gift from my grandmother 50 years ago. OK, it had square root and a built-in value of π , so that made things a tad more efficient. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: If we ever discover something that defied the laws of physics, would we be adding a new topic in physics or questioning whether or not our laws and ideas in physics were all wrong?
Answer: Throughout the history of modern science, progress was made when we discovered something that defined the laws of physics known at the time. These challenges were met by making sense of what we saw, and ultimately, revising and improving our understanding of Nature. The “laws of physics” are not dogma, not some unchanging commandments from the deities of the physical sciences or anything like that. They simply reflect our present understanding of how Nature works. Challenges are welcome, especially when they are unexpected, as it is thanks to those challenges that progress is made. No, progress does not mean questioning whether our ideas “were all wrong”. We know that they are not all wrong: our ideas have been well tested through observation and experiment and they have a very good track record, successfully predicting results. So they cannot be “all wrong”. That does not mean that they are the final word on any particular topic. Take classical mechanics, for instance. It all seemed so nice and simple, back in the 18th century. But then, those pesky engineers invented steam engines. Engines producing mechanical energy out of… what exactly? Heat? What is heat? How is it related to motion? It took decades before physicists began to make sense of all this, after exploring some remarkable detours, eventually discarding concepts like caloricum and finally arriving at modern formulations of axiomatic thermodynamics and statistical physics. Or how about the luminiferous ether theory, which made perfect sense in light of Maxwell’s equations… that is, until it didn’t, in light of the famous (and, by the standards of the day, very surprising) Michelson-Morley null result, eventually leading to relativity theory? Or how about Rutherford’s surprising result? Bombard a thin gold foil with alpha particles. They should pass through with minimal deflection, according to the then-popular model of the atom, Thomson’s. But they didn’t. Some of the alpha particles were actually reflected! To quote Rutherford, “It was almost as incredible as if you fired a 15-inch shell at a piece of tissue paper and it came back and hit you.” And sure, it led to a major revision of our understanding of atoms, another step in the early 20th century towards modern particle physics. So you see, surprising discoveries happen all the time. We love them! They let us learn something new. As to how we respond to them, it depends on the nature of the discovery. Sometimes, it opens a whole new chapter in physics (e.g., thermodynamics, relativity theory, quantum theory). Sometimes it leads to a refinement or improved understanding within an existing framework (e.g., Rutherford’s atomic model). In all cases, it means we can take another meaningful step forward. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does a mass know in which direction to move in order to bend space-time?
Answer: A mass doesn’t “know” anything, it doesn’t need to move, and it doesn’t bend space-time. Other than that… Okay, allow me to explain. To be a source of gravitation, a mass does not need to move. The simple presence of mass (energy-momentum, to be precise) acts as a source of gravitation. Masses in the gravitational field of another mass do move, but in their case, the direction of motion is determined by the gravitational field itself: they accelerate in the direction of steepest change (i.e., “downward”). And no, mass does not bend spacetime. It is the source of the gravitational field. The gravitational field is “universal”, which means it affects everything the same way, no exceptions. As a consequence, it can be interpreted as a change in the geometry of spacetime. This interpretation can be helpful, can be useful, but only if we never forget that, interpretations notwithstanding, the gravitational field is just as physical a field as the electromagnetic field, e.g., carrying energy and momentum from place to place in the form of gravitational waves, just as the electromagnetic field carries energy and momentum from place to place in the form of electromagnetic waves (e.g., light). (As a reminder, Einstein himself cautioned us against taking the geometric interpretation too literally.) Lastly, even if we do interpret the gravitational field as geometry, we must keep in mind that it truly is spacetime geometry. So much so that, e.g., in the case of the gravitational field of the Earth, spatial curvature contributes only about one part in a billion. Or to put it differently, what we know as Newtonian gravity is due entirely to the rate at which clocks tick in a gravitational field; the relativistic correction due to spatial curvature is only a tiny, one-part-in-a-billion adjustment of the Newtonian value.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Is it true that everything travels at a constant velocity in deep space, near the speed of light?
Answer: No, it is not true. First of all, in the context of relativity theory, it is important to remember that the concept of speed is relative. Things do not travel at some velocity, nor do that stay put. Things travel relative to other things. To give you an example that dates back to Galileo: Suppose you are on a sailing ship, sitting in a windowless cabin as the ship sails on perfectly smooth seas. You are staring at a glass on the table in front of you. The glass is not moving. Or is it? How could you even tell? Relative to you, the glass is at rest. Relative to the shore, it moves at some velocity (how fast do medieval sailing ships move anyway?) along with you and the table and the rest of the ship. But relative to the Sun? It moves about 30 kilometers every second! Or how about relative to the central region of the Milky Way? We’re now up to roughly 200 km/s. And then relative to some really distant objects in deep space, you, your glass and the table it sits own, your ship, the Earth, the Sun, the Milky Way all move at a speed close to the vacuum speed of light. And it goes both ways. From your perspective, it’s not you or the Earth that is moving so fast, but the distant galaxy! However, if there are aliens on that galaxy, they’d say it’s you who is moving and they’re the ones standing still. So as I said, motion is relative. And constant it is not. If there were no forces (including gravity) acting on objects, motion (relative as it is) would always be in a straight line at constant velocity. But there are forces. Gravity in particular (a force that we often interpret geometrically) alters the trajectories of objects. So they no longer move in a straight line or at a constant speed relative to other things. The Earth moves around the Sun, and its Sun-relative velocity changes in magnitude, too, as its orbit is elliptical. The velocity of the Earth relative to, say, Mars, is even more twisted. These specific examples notwithstanding if there is one thing that is worth remembering, it’s that velocity is always relative. That applies even to light in a vacuum. The magnitude of its velocity is the same for all observers, but the direction in which a light ray travels is different in different observer reference frames. (In fact, if you look up the concept of aberration in astronomy, this has been known since before relativity theory, for over 300 years as a matter of fact).

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Isn't a supernova an instantaneous event? Why is it said that the last supernova was visible in the sky for 23 days? Shouldn't the explosion only be seen for some seconds?
Answer: Have you seen motion pictures of large explosions? Nuclear tests? The actual explosion is as instantaneous as they come: it’s over in milliseconds or less. Yet in the first millisecond, you don’t even see much. It takes several seconds, minutes even, for the gigantic fireball to flare up, grow, reach its maximum brightness and eventually fade. And that’s a man-made explosion. Large by the standards of us lowly humans, but absolutely nothing compared to a supernova. An explosion that involves several times the mass of the Sun (i.e., several million times the mass of the Earth). An explosion that heats up this material to astonishing temperatures, causing it to fly apart in a gigantic fireball. So don’t be surprised if the light curve reaches its maximum only hours, or more likely, days after the actual event (depending on the type and size of the supernova); and especially don’t be surprised that it then takes weeks or months for the remnant to fade, as the fireball grows in size and becomes fainter. And of course it never quite goes away: e.g., here are the remnants of a fireball that was observed by Chinese astronomers 970 years ago, in 1054: It’s the famous Crab Nebula. Not visible to the naked eye, sure, but still there if you know where to look with a backyard telescope. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Does the space bend like this: The closer to the center of the mass you are, the smaller it is, things tending to go where it is smaller, explaining gravity?
Answer: No. What we experience as Newtonian gravity is primarily related to the rate of clocks. The stronger the gravitational field, the slower clocks tick in it compared to other clocks in deep space. This results in altered trajectories, objects falling onto, or orbiting, other objects. Spatial effects of relativity theory only begin to play a substantial role when either the gravitational field is very strong (neutron stars and beyond) or the particles probing the field move near the vacuum speed of light. In fact, this leads to Einstein’s famous prediction that particles of light, i.e., photons, will have trajectories near a mass that would be deflected by twice the amount one would calculate using Newtonian gravity alone. This prediction was first confirmed by Eddington’s famous expedition in 1919, observing a solar eclipse and the slight displacement, visible during the eclipse, of stars that appear in the sky near the Sun. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: What effect does gravity have on a photon moving directly away from a massive object?
Answer: You stumbled upon one of the three “classical tests” of general relativity theory proposed by Einstein when the theory was new. The other two are the anomalous perihelion advance of Mercury and the bending of rays of light by a gravitating body. This one, however, is about redshift. Namely that rays of light, photons, arriving from a “deep gravitational well”, will appear to have lost energy. Key to understanding this is gravitational time dilation: remembering that a “perfect clock” appears to tick more slowly when in a gravitational field, compared to an identical clock that is far from any gravitational source. So then, imagine a ray of light, say, a very blue/violet ray of light with a wavelength of 400 nm leaving the surface of a compact, heavy object. Suppose that the object is so heavy, clocks there appear to tick at a rate that is 2/3rd the rate of a clock in deep space, far from sources of gravitation. That 400 nm light ray corresponds to an electromagnetic field that oscillates 750 trillion times a second (750 THz). That is, 750 trillion oscillations while a clock near the light source counts 1 second. Now imagine someone in deep space detecting this light ray. That person uses his own clock to measure time. and his own clock appears to tick faster. While the clock on the surface of the object counted 1 second, this clock in deep space will have counted 3/2 times 1 second, which is to say, one and a half seconds. So it takes one and a half seconds to receive those 750 trillion oscillations. Which means that in one second, this detector will have seen only 500 trillion oscillations. That is to say, it will have observed that light ray at 500 THz, not 750 THz. The corresponding wavelength, then, is not 400 nm but 600 nm. What started off as very blue light arrives at the detector as light that appears very much more like orange. And this, then, is the effect of gravity on a photon. As it climbs out of the “gravity well”, the photon loses energy, which is to say, its characteristic frequency shifts down, the corresponding wavelength increasing. Question: What if the singularity in the middle of a black hole was another black hole. As the mass squeezed down to a point going in then singularity goes to a black hole?
Answer: OK, here is the problem: there is no singularity in the “middle” of a black hole. The singularity inside the event horizon of a Schwarzschild black hole is not some spot in the middle. As a matter of fact, the interior of the event horizon of a collapsing cloud of matter is well described by the same homogeneous and isotropic solution that describes an expanding or collapsing universe (see, e.g., Weinberg’s 1972 Gravitation and Cosmology, sec. 11.9). The singularity in this mini-universe is not a place; it is an inevitable future moment in time. So no, it’s not another black hole. It’s the “end of time”, end-of-the-world moment insofar as observers trapped inside the event horizon are concerned. If you find my posts useful, please consider supporting my efforts.

Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why is a true “random number generator” impossible?
Answer: Given the large number of answers already offered to this question (many of which are quite sensible, actually) I hesitate to add my own voice. Still, perhaps it is warranted. That is because I feel compelled to begin my answer with a question myself: What is "random" in this context? What would be the criteria by which we consider a random number generator to be a) “good”, b) "true"? What does "good" mean if I need a random number generator to do a Monte Carlo simulation representing a physics problem? Why, I want the sequence of numbers to be free of any obvious autocorrelation: future numbers should not be trivially predictable from recent numbers. Repetitive patterns are a bad thing, as they can either mask or amplify real physics. For instance, if I were to use a random number generator to simulate a physical system emitting or absorbing radiation, I'd like to be assured that when I see a peak at a specific frequency, it's real physics, not an artifact of a bad random number generator. On the other hand, I don't mind at all if the sequence of "random" numbers is deterministic: Quite the contrary, this is actually Good News, because it allows me to have repeatable numerical experiments! It also allows me to test how sensitive my system is to the random number sequences themselves; e.g., a machine learning neural network may be quite sensitive to how its cells are initialized using different sets of random numbers so I can repeat experiments using different seed values with the same random number generator, to see how the network responds. But then, there is cryptography. There, too, the desire is to have random numbers that are unpredictable, but the "unpredictable" part means something quite different. Autocorrelation may not be of great concern when relatively short sequences are generated (e.g., a 1024-bit random key). But we want to make sure that the result cannot be predicted from related information. Simply using a good random number generator algorithm is not good enough. A hacker might guess which algorithm was used. In fact, if the software is open source, they don't even need to guess. So we need something else: a "truly" random seed value. Something that is not generated by any deterministic algorithm. As these two examples demonstrate, what constitutes a good random number generator depends on the application. In the case of a physics simulation, we are perfectly okay with a deterministic algorithm (in fact, it may be a desirable feature!), so long as the sequence it generates has the desired statistical properties. In the case of a cryptographic application, while statistical goodness is important, it's even more important that the generation of random numbers must be non-deterministic, so that its output cannot be predicted even when all details about the system are available. Modern operating systems offer the best of both worlds. There are algorithms, software libraries for high-quality deterministic random number generation, which can be used effectively in physics, machine learning, etc., problems. There are also options to generate "hardware" random numbers from sources of "randomness" that can include anything from the system clock to user actions to random, unpredictable bits from network traffic or the computer hardware itself. However, collecting enough "entropy" can be time consuming, so hardware random numbers are often used as seed values for a deterministic random number generator, instead of being used directly. It is, of course, also possible to create dedicated hardware generating random noise. Question: Light is deflected by gravity. But look at this explanation: Why is there deflection of starlight in the Newtonian model? Shouldn't it simply be straight? https://qrcd.org/5VmM Reply
Answer: Newtonian gravity would predict a deflection if light if light consisted of particles. Newtonian gravity, however, does not predict a similar deflection if light is described as a wave theory, namely as electromagnetic radiation in Maxwell’s theory. General relativity, in contrast, predicts a deflection in both cases. Moreover, the deflection it predicts is twice the deflection that one would predict using Newtonian gravity. That is because, to get a bit more technical, in addition to the temporal part of the metric tensor (which is what’s behind Newtonian gravity) for anything moving at or near the vacuum speed of light, the spatial part offers an equal contribution, doubling the deflection. This is why the deflection of light was offered as a crucial test of general relativity, and why Eddington’s 1919 solar eclipse expedition, which confirmed Einstein’s prediction, was so important. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Why is light a particle and a wave at the same time? Can you explain the two slot experiment?
Answer: “Wave-particle duality” is another one of those unfortunate phrases that are invented to help explain a difficult concept, but do more harm than good in the end. So here is the thing when it comes to quantum phenomena: the exact outcome of a measurement, carried out using a classical instrument (say, the human eyeball) cannot be predicted. We can only predict probabilities. But it’s not like “classical” probabilities. The limitation does not arise from the fact that we lack full knowledge of the system. Rather, the exact outcome of an experiment does not exist until, well, until it exists. It is not some technological limitation: it is not predictable in principle. But then… what can we predict? We can predict probabilities. And these probabilities are governed by an equation that, for all practical intents and purposes, travel like a wave. Waves that interfere with one another. Waves that reinforce or cancel one another at various places. In the end, though we do not observe these waves. We observe, say, the impact of a photon. There! A particle, making its appearance at a specific place, say, a specific point on your retina when you see a brief flash of light. But “en route”, there was no particle. We cannot identify the path that the particle traveled in order to reach its destination because no such path exists. What we can do is explore that “probability wave” as it “travels” from source to destination. This allows us to assign specific probabilities as to where the “particle” might be observed when it comes to that. So you see… that thing we observe is really not a particle: a particle, like a miniature cannonball, would follow a well-defined trajectory, and in this case, no such trajectory exists. But that thing we observe is really not a wave either. The “wave” in question is a mathematical abstraction, a probability amplitude, not a “thing”. The “thing” is the impact of the photon on your retina, which is particle-like behavior, but again, a true particle would have a path associated with it. And it is this point that I need to offer a reminder that, like it or not, quantum physics cannot be intuited. It is outside the ability of the human mind to intuit these things, just as, say, a language model like GPT cannot “intuit” an image or a sound, as it lacks the ability to process images or sounds. It can still reason about them, but that reasoning requires discipline and, well, knowledge of mathematics. We are in the same shoes here: With our scientific discipline and mathematical tools, we can make robust predictions about the quantum world. But we make these predictions precisely because we let go of our desire to intuit the quantum world and instead, chose to follow the math (verified by experiment, of course). So that’s my advice: Do not take this “wave-particle” business literally, as an invitation to try to intuit the unintuitable. Or if you must, at least remind yourself that the “wave” is a probability wave (not a physical thing), and the “particle” is not really a particle with a definite path, even if in the end, when we observe it (but only then!) it may masquerade as one. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: Can Viktor Toth explain this statement of his: Newtonian gravity is due almost entirely to how the presence of mass-energy alters the rate of clock?
Answer: In general relativity, gravitational is a tensor quantity. A tensor quantity can be represented by a matrix. A matrix that we interpret as the metric of spacetime, determining the geometric relationships in both space and in time between events. One particular term in this matrix is about the rate of clocks. The other terms characterize movement and stretching distances. In the case of weak fields and slow velocities, general relativity’s predictions become indistinguishable from Newtonian gravity. When we take a close look as to why, we find that in that matrix, pretty much all the terms become insignificant, with one exception: the one that determines the rate at which clocks tick. This term becomes, in the Newtonian approximation, none other than the Newtonian gravitational potential. So if we map the gravitational potential of a system, what we actually map is the rate at which clocks tick at various places in that system. Conversely, if we had a family of stationary clocks all over a system, comparing the rates at which they tick would allow us to reconstruct the gravitational field. If the field becomes strong, or if things begin to move close to the speed of light, all this changes. This is why, for instance, rays of light near the Sun bend twice as much as they would under Newtonian gravity. For particles like photons, moving at the vacuum speed of light, spatial curvature has an effect just as large as gravitational time dilation on their trajectory. But for things at nonrelativistic velocities, in “weak” gravitational fields (and by “weak”, I mean anything not quite approaching the insane surface gravity of a neutron star) time dilation and the gravitational potential are essentially the same thing. Name: Viktor T. Toth
Question: How does a black hole maintain its structure despite its density and mass?
Answer: I think this question implies a misunderstanding of what a black hole really is. Allow me to distinguish between two “black holes”: When an astrophysical object collapses, the collapse never actually ends insofar as outside observers are concerned. The infalling material approaches, but never quite reaches, the famous event horizon; in fact, the event horizon’s very formation remains forever in any outside observer’s future. This is a result of ever increasing gravitational time dilation, as a result of which to outside observers, the collapse occurs in ever increasing slow motion. In fact, this is implied already by the title of the famous 1939 paper by Oppenheimer and Snyder that first described this process: “On Continued Gravitational Contraction”. So there really is no structure to maintain; on the contrary the collapse happens precisely because an object (e.g., a heavy star at the end of its life, having run out of fuel) cannot maintain its structure. The end state, e.g., a Schwarzschild black hole, is mathematics, not physics, at least insofar as outside observers are concerned. It represents the state that the collapsing object approaches, but never quite reaches (due to time dilation). An infalling observer, however, would reach and cross the horizon in finite time as measured by his own clock. This observer would find himself in a collapsing mini-universe, and his future would be sealed: Depending on the size of the black hole, it could be milliseconds or hours or days, but ultimately, his existence will come to an end. (At least in the spherically symmetric Schwarzschild case.) So again, there is no structure that would be maintained; the collapse continues until its bitter end. Question: What does "non-local literally mean? Why is it important? How did Bell's theorem prove it?
Answer: Bell’s theorem offers insight into how quantum nonlocality works by looking at how distant events in quantum physics are correlated in ways that cannot happen in the classical world. But first, allow me to offer the “classic” classical example: socks. Suppose you travel. You pack your favorite pair of socks. Upon arrival in your hotel room in a distant land, you unpack and realize that only half the pair is present in your suitcase. You instantly gain knowledge that the other half is back at home, thousands of miles away, in your socks drawer. No magic here, of course. Although you only just observed it, the information was there all along. It was in the form of a “local” (carried with you all along) “hidden” (in your suitcase) variable. So now let’s take a look at a quantum physics experiment. We send two particles (say, two electrons) in different directions. The electrons are correlated: their total angular momentum is zero. We then measure both electrons at their respective arrival locations. If the spin of one of them is “up”, the other will be “down”, as expected. Conservation laws are, after all, strict and absolute. So far so good, this is just like the aforementioned socks. But now we introduce a twist. We now change the orientation of one of the measurement devices a little. The two receiving locations are no longer parallel, so we do not expect perfect correlation. But we do expect some correlation. Quantum physics predicts a correlation between the two locations that is just “too good” in a sense. It cannot be explained by classical physics, by local hidden variables. The electron at one of the locations somehow “knows” what the electron at the other location is doing, despite the distance between them, despite the fact that it’s not even clear which electron is measured first, as that depends on who is looking (i.e., the relativistic reference frame in which we describe the experiment). This is the essence of the mathematical statement that is known as Bell’s inequality. Conservation laws in quantum physics are generally like this. You cannot nail them down to any particular location or moment in time, but when you look at a quantum system that is isolated from its environment, it always obeys conservation laws exactly (no probabilities here, conservation laws are exact). Question: If motion is non-absolute, why are we looking for dark energy when energy isn't required for a 'perceptually'-expanding universe?
Answer: Don’t be misled by a name. “Dark energy” is neither “dark” nor “energy”. Blame physicists for coming up with inappropriate names and sticking with them long after they exhausted their usefulness. (The inappropriate names, not the physicists.) It’s called “dark” when in fact it should be called “invisible”. Or “completely transparent, not interacting with known forms of matter or light”. But… okay, “dark”. As to “energy”, well, insofar as general relativity is concerned, at least in the context of cosmology, everything is “energy”: that is, everything is characterized by its energy-content and pressure. Which is to say, everything in a non-empty universe is assumed to be well approximated by the concept of an “isotropic perfect fluid”. So “dark energy” is really a “completely transparent, non-interacting medium with negative pressure, characterized by the equation of state p = − ρ , “ which is to say, its pressure is the negative of its energy density. Contrast this with “dark matter”, which is a “completely transparent, non-interacting medium with no pressure.” Sometimes also called “dust”. Motion has nothing to do with it. The equations of cosmology match observations (in particular, minute fluctuations of the cosmic microwave background and the large-scale statistical distribution of matter) if the universe is roughly 70% “dark energy” and 30% “dust” (which also includes ordinary matter, by the way, since its pressure is negligible compared to relativistic mediums.) As to the expansion, nothing perceptual about it. Things are flying apart. Not something abstract like “the universe”, or “space” or the “cosmos”. Literally, things: galaxies, clusters of galaxies are flying apart, which is to say, the average distance between them increases over time, their density decreasing over time. Question: Since the Bekenstein Bound and BH event horizons are the most information dense places possible, how probable is it that they are conscious?
Answer: I think this question was inspired, in part, by a misconception of the meaning, “information”. Allow me to show two character sequences of approximately equal length. First, this: To be, or not to be: that is the question: Whether 'tis nobler in the mind to suffer The slings and arrows of outrageous fortune, Or to take arms against a sea of troubles. And now this: 8RfUd8yHHftN5juY5MPME1SxwcE7lNOAjjo6Q1jlKyK0hdwk 8DU86TeOGcyJZ1Gk2cEMAtRlBK1G0Sy1WU2xFwJ4sBCeQv15 qBV4pJKGcY28npr4GBDXoJQ1aHw09P9xGrJMqjJ3Jj8pXRWO C5jUXwiEWn2cLNFH91Qxnws3 Which of these contain more “information”? It is understandable if you thought it was the first example. The second case is, after all, just some printable ASCII gibberish, no useful content whatsoever. But that does not mean no information! In fact, if you feed both examples to compression algorithms, you will find that the algorithm does a much better job compressing Shakespeare’s lines than the random sequence of letters. In the end, significantly fewer bytes, significantly less information is needed to fully reconstruct the first example compared to the second. But we don’t even need abstract algorithms. Let me show you what I mean: To b, or nt to b: tht s th qstn: Whethr 'ts noblr in th mnd to suffr Th slngs nd arrws of outrgs frtne, Or to tk arms gnst a sea of trbls. Look at this text. I am betting that if you are a native English speaker, you have no trouble reading it even though almost 20% of the letters are missing. You can still unambiguously reconstruct the original. In contrast, if I were to remove but a single letter from the second example containing gibberish, you’d have no way of knowing what that letter was. There is no redundancy. Everything there is important information. We tend to associate information with order. We think there is more information in, say, in a picture on the CRT of an old-fashioned analog television set as opposed to the “snow” we see when the channel is not broadcasting. But in reality, the opposite is true: random noise carries a lot more information than an orderly broadcast. Of course no one said that that information is of any use. Put enough monkeys behind typewriters and the result may even include the four lines of Shakespeare above. But it will also include all other possible combinations of 170-odd letters and symbols, and you’d have no way of knowing what is useful and what is not. So no, a black hole’s event horizon is not conscious. If anything, it’s the opposite. Imagine your brain scrambled in a food processor. The result represents a lot more “information”!
